pages.text: Ten Turkey Facts to Gobble Up This Thanksgiving | Smithsonian Voices | National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute Smithsonian Magazine Skip to main content National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute Ten Turkey Facts to Gobble Up This Thanksgiving Dive into the juicy history of America’s favorite barnyard bird Mike Bock November 13, 2026 Get our Newsletter! Get our Newsletter! Like many birds, domestic turkeys, including this group at the Smithsonian's National Zoo in Washington, D.C., are social animals. Smithsonian/Brett Kuxhausen 1. Humans have been raising turkeys for thousands of years. Although indigenous peoples in North America have hunted wild turkeys since the end of the last Ice Age, the animals were first domesticated in Mexico around 2,000 years ago. Dinner wasn’t the original goal: archaeological evidence suggests turkeys were initially kept so their feathers could be used in clothing and ceremonial regalia. By A.D. 500, people were raising turkeys in what is now the United States too, judging by archaeological remains from caves in Arizona and New Mexico. Even so, those weren’t the birds that English settlers ate in the Thirteen Colonies. The domestic turkey descends from a southern Mexican bird that the Spanish took home in the 1500s. The birds then spread through Europe, and colonists brought them back across the Atlantic. The bird’s English name may reflect this long-distance trade: turkeys are thought to have reached England along winding trading routes that first passed through the country of Turkey. 2. pages.title: Thawing Permafrost May Have Created a New Type of Landslide, Which Could Become More Common as the World Warms
pages.description: Scientists call the events permafrost detachment slides. Instead of thawing from the top down, these landslides seem to originate from a weakened base
pages.text: Thawing Permafrost May Have Created a New Type of Landslide, Which Could Become More Common as the World Warms Skip to main content A scar left by the 2018 Redstone River permafrost landslide, one of the two events investigated in the new study. Adapted from J. M. Young et al., Geophysical Research Letters , 2026 In 2017 and 2018, a pair of strange landslides moved huge masses of rock and dirt in Canada’s Northwest Territories. The events occurred in the central Mackenzie Valley, and one of them even dammed a river and created a lake . The two natural disasters are part of a new class of landslides scientists are calling “permafrost detachment slides” in a study published in the journal Geophysical Research Letters in September. They may have been partially triggered by severe wildfires that occurred in 1995, which destabilized the ground and allowed the base of the permafrost to thaw. What’s more, these events may become more common as the planet continues to warm. “It’s a very dramatic manifestation of the changing climate,” says study co-author Joseph Young , a geoscientist who conducted the work at the University of Alberta in Canada, to Matt Simon at Grist . “They’ve only started happening in the last 10, 15 years, and it’s a very drastic and abrupt change in the landscape.” Young and his colleagues began the study after seeing something strange in the Northwest Territories in 2019. While conducting field research, they spotted large landslide scars in valleys that they knew were stable permafrost , or permanently frozen earth, reports Stephanie Pappas for Live Science

Learn about other national symbols. History of the American flag The flag of the United States is a symbol of freedom before which Americans recite the pledge of allegiance . The flag's 13 red and white stripes represent the 13 original colonies. Its 50 white stars on a blue background represent the 50 states. Each of the colors on the flag has a meaning: Red: valor and bravery White: purity and innocence Blue: vigilance, perseverance, and justice A star is added to the flag when a new state joins the United States. The flag was last modified on July 4, 1960, when Hawaii was incorporated as a state. Learn more about the evolution of the American flag and its earlier designs. How to raise the flag Follow these guidelines to properly display the American flag [PDF, 162KB]. When to fly the flag at half-staff The American flag flies at half-staff or at half-mast when the country or a state is in mourning. The president, a state governor, or the mayor of the District of Columbia can order flags to fly at half-staff. In the foothills, access routes to the mines ran through an area called Nok. Over the years, with the exploitation of the mines and the local people who overwhelmingly provided the labor force, numerous fragments of ancient pottery came to light but were largely ignored. One piece, too striking to be disregarded, appeared in 1928: a small monkey head, sculpted in terra-cotta. The mine manager, Lt. Col. John Dent Young, had that piece and other fragments transferred to a museum in the city of Jos, the provincial capital. Fifteen years later, a miner found another terra-cotta head and took it home, where he used it as a scarecrow, apparently with some success. Reed stylus in her hand, she pressed its tiny wedge-shaped tip into the clay to build the small, spiky characters of cuneiform. Alaska has the only Arctic parks in the National Park System, and together, those parks make up more than a quarter of the total amount of land managed by the National Park Service. The boundary of the Arctic is the Arctic Circle, an imaginary line around the Earth (at about 66.5° North Latitude) where, for at least one day each year, the sun does not completely set (June 21) or rise (December 22). pages.text: The Artisans Trying to Bring Back Neolithic Fashion | National Geographic Premium HISTORY & CULTURE The Artisans Trying to Bring Back Neolithic Fashion A growing community of craftspeople are trying to build knowledge of ancient clothing—by making it themselves. Historical craft specialist Vasi Birchwood recreates fashion from the Neolithic period on her Youtube channel. This outfit is one of her creations. The jacket is made of deer skin, stitched with deer skin cord and a bone awl, and adorned with moose teeth. The shirt underneath the jacket is made of undyed linen, hand stitched with linen thread. The skirt is made of deer skin and decorated with braided hemp strings. Photo Illustration: NGM Staff; Source Photos for Illustration: Vasi Birchwood By Starre Vartan Published November 2, 2026 Around the fire, no one seems especially bothered by the rain. Some people duck beneath bark shelters to continue twisting cordage from plant fibers. Others cook foraged plants or work leather while steam rises from damp clothing. A few wander into the drizzle to gather more wood before returning to the warmth of the flames. Among them is historical craft specialist and YouTube educator Vasi Birchwood . For Birchwood, weather isn't an inconvenience so much as another participant in this meeting of experiential archeologists and craft experts in Northern Germany. That shift in perspective is just one of the many ways she does more than dress like a Neolithic person at these gatherings. The continent of North America has been inhabited by humans for at least 16,500 years. As early as the 1500s, early settlers and European thinkers were interested in discovering how humans had come to populate North and South America. One theory suggested the migration of Norsemen across Greenland into North America. Another theory proposed the island of Atlantis as the origins of human life in the New World. Yet another idea proposed that the inhabitants had generated out of mud. However, by the early 1800s, scientists and theorists began discussing the possibility of a land bridge that had spanned between Asia and North America thousands of years ago. Dan Zaffra By Amy Brecount White Published January 14, 2026 Where was I when a magenta aurora borealis could be seen as far south as Florida? Indoors and not paying enough attention. Thankfully, there are multiple apps for that. “Many visitors come to Dark Sky Parks for a chance to see the Milky Way, since 80 percent of Americans can't see it from their hometown,” says Jackie Rabb, a Mesa Verde National Park ranger and night sky lead at this certified International Dark Sky Park . Knowable Magazine Whether it’s gushing from a bumped nose or pooling atop a pricked finger, our blood is some hue of red. But red-bloodedness isn’t universal in the animal kingdom. In some creatures, the vital fluid is purple; in others it’s yellow, green or even white. What imparts these different colors to the liquid of life? To find out, Knowable magazine waded into the research and spoke with a couple of scientists who have studied the stuff. Here’s what’s known about the science behind the hues. Bizarre blues and purples The rich red of vertebrate blood comes from hemoglobin, a protein in red blood cells that contains iron atoms. Hemoglobin’s job is to deliver oxygen—and its iron atoms, which grab onto oxygen, make our blood look red. pages.text: The Complicated Social Life of a Tyrannosaurus Rex | National Geographic SCIENCE Why Everything We Thought We Knew About T. Rex is Getting … Messier Fossil evidence has shifted our view of T. rex from a complete loner tyrant into a more nuanced carnivore. Scarred skulls, scraped ground, and fossilized trackways suggest adult tyrannosaurs lived largely solitary lives, like modern big cats, but also gathered in communal display arenas to woo potential mates. GERD LUDWIG, National Geographic Image Collection By Riley Black Published October 8, 2026 Every time I’m in New York, I have to visit her. She’s always waiting in the same place, standing on the fourth floor of the American Museum of Natural History, grinning so wide that her teeth gleam under the bright lights. Experts know her as AMNH 5027. I know her as the first T yrannosaurus rex I ever met. Before the discovery of “Sue,” “Stan,” “Scotty,” and many other famous skeletons of Earth’s last great carnivorous dinosaur, AMNH 5027 was the icon. The partial skeleton was the first T . rex to include a complete skull – only slightly smushed. It left no doubt that the dinosaur was an impressive flesh-ripper, reconstructed with jaws agape when the museum’s paleontologists assembled real bones and casts in the world’s first great introduction to the dinosaur. (And, when Michael Crichton’s Jurassic Park needed a skeletal dinosaur for the cover, AMNH 5027 was the model.) SCIENCE LAELAPS The Echoes of Toothed Birds By Riley Black Published May 22, 2015 • 4 min read Whenever I spot a grebe, I try to imagine the bird with teeth. This is another symptom of a chronically fossiliferous mind. You see, these snake-necked swimming birds have traditionally been taken as a proxy for a specific sort of ancient avian called hesperornithiforms. Best known by, as you might guess, Hesperornis – these toothed birds pioneered the diving lifestyle between 113 and 66 million years ago. Today’s grebes and loons look like edentulous echos of these lost Cretaceous days, or, as beautifully expressed by ornithologist William Beebe : When in the depth of the winter, a full hundred miles from the nearest land, one sees a loon in the path of the steamer, listens to its weird, maniacal laughter, and sees it slowly sink downward through the green waters, it truly seems a hint of the bird-life of long-past ages. No surprise, then, that paleontologists past sometimes considered loons and grebes to be the descendants of Hesperornis . Their bones carry the same superficial similarity. But this is an evolutionary ruse known as convergence. Loons and grebes are copycats that independently took up the same lifestyle as the toothed birds that dove after fish in warm Cretaceous seas and sometimes wound up in the stomachs of monstrous marine reptiles. Steps include the president creating the budget plan and Congress’s work creating funding bills for the president to sign. Annual funding areas Every year, the U.S. Congress begins work on a federal budget for the next fiscal year. The federal government’s fiscal year runs from October 1 of one calendar year through September 30 of the next. And the annual budget covers three spending areas: Mandatory spending - funding for Social Security, Medicare, veterans benefits, and other spending required by law. This typically uses over half of all funding. Discretionary spending - federal agency funding. Congress sets funding levels for these each year. This usually accounts for around a third of all funding. Interest on the debt - this usually uses less than 10 percent of all funding. Creating the U.S. federal budget The budget planning begins a year before the budget is to go into effect. Federal agencies create budget requests and submit them to the White House Office of Management and Budget (OMB). OMB refers to the agencies’ requests as it develops the budget proposal for the president. The president submits the budget proposal to Congress early the next year. Others too small to gain much notice from the paleontologists who were set on finding large, imposing specimens for museum centerpieces. Whatever the reasons, though, a big, heavily-armored dinosaur was able to escape the notice of paleontologists despite over a century of Jurassic exploration. North America’s Morrison Formation is a fossiliferous wonderland. Spectacular bonebeds dot its reach from Canada to Mexico, and it was one of the focal points for the great Bone Wars between O.C. Yann Garin By Lauren Paige Richeson Published October 15, 2026 Long before our messages arrived with a buzz, a letter could introduce itself by touch. Without even glimpsing the handwriting inside, the paper itself announced a family name, a profession, a crest, or a ceremony—not merely a decoration, but a declaration. In Paris, one of the most refined ways to create that impression was with timbrage au balancier , or pendulum stamping. Developed in the 19th-century world of engraving and correspondence, the technique gave calling cards, invitations, letterheads, and envelope flaps something ordinary ink could not provide: a feeling. Everything from a coat of arms to a pair of initials could rise from the page in dense color and varying depths. But as correspondence slipped from paper to pixels and luxury printing pressed faster towards mechanized processes, the manual craft began to lose the world that sustained it. From roughly the 16th to 19th centuries, much of the Earth was gripped by a persistent frigid cold. It left ripples through history—and some lessons for today’s climate crisis. By Kieran Mulvaney Published February 20, 2024 Thousands of people walking and playing across the frozen River Thames. Soldiers on horseback capturing ships stuck in the ice. Indigenous populations using snowshoes to outfox English interlopers. Accused witches put on trial as their communities struggled to explain crop failures and extreme cold. These were some of the images that define the Little Ice Age—a period of several centuries last millennium in which parts of the Northern Hemisphere grappled with a persistent cold. But what caused the Little Ice Age, how long did it last, how did people adapt to its frigid grip—and what lessons can we learn as we enter our own period of climatic change? ( Broken Baculum a Sign of Painful Ice Age Injury) What is the Little Ice Age—and what caused it? The Black Paintings Titled “Atropos” (“The Fates”), this work by Francisco de Goya shows a man bound at the mercy of the three Fates, or Moirai, the goddesses of Greek mythology who spun the thread of destiny, measured and allotted it, and cut it short. pages.text: The secret lives of forgotten ancient Greeks | National Geographic By Candida Moss Published July 31, 2026 Stones & Bones is back! Today, we visit an excavation underway in Greece that may reshape what we know about its ancient past. Want to make sure you get every Stones & Bones newsletter? Put your email here . More than two millennia ago, young girls from the Greek countryside used to travel every four years to the Sanctuary of Artemis at Brauron outside Athens, to participate in a mysterious rite of passage. They went there, one ancient participant enigmatically said, to “play the bear.” Guided by the priestesses of Artemis and out of sight of their fathers and brothers, the girls ran free, embodying the bear as part of a ritual that allowed them to shed their wildness and prepare for marriage. Painted cups found at the site that were possibly made by participants themselves show girls running and dancing. They would return later in life to dedicate offerings to the goddess in preparation for childbirth. One day in the third century B.C., the sanctuary was abandoned forever. And no one knows why. pages.text: The Surprising Secret Weapon Against Spotted Lanternflies | National Geographic Premium ANIMALS The Surprising Secret Weapon Against Spotted Lanternflies Early research suggests that a backyard plant might poison the invasive species. Scientists are studying a promising way to control the spread of the invasive spotted lanternfly with a common plant. Mark Mirko, Connecticut Public/Getty Images By Jason Bittel Published September 1, 2026 The spotted lanternfly is a large, visually striking insect that first showed up in the U.S. in 2014. In just over a decade, this invasive species has multiplied across the American Northeast, with new range expansions into the Midwest and South, bringing the total number of states where they can now be found to 19, as well as the District of Columbia. Not only do they feed on plant sap and harm trees, but spotted lanternflies also pose a threat to the grape and wine industry , among many other crops. Scientists have recently said that squashing them likely won’t make a dent in their populations. However, they may have stumbled upon a new weapon in the fight against the invasive species—one that just so happens to be critical habitat for monarch butterflies , an insect species perhaps as loved as the lanternfly is despised: Milkweed. When spotted lanternflies feed on the stuff, they have a tendency to drop dead. “We were planning to run the experiment for a week, except when we went back the next day, the majority of the lanternflies that were on milkweed were dead,” says Anne Johnson , a postdoctoral researcher at Michigan State University.

See more digitized stories from our archives here . I still recall the dredges and the bulldozers working in the red mangrove swamps near my father's house. I never thought their destruction was much of a loss. Mangroves were scrub: junk trees. The peculiar aerial roots, which, like spidery legs, prop the mangroves up in the mud, made the swamps seem forbidding. Swarms of mosquitoes and clicking, crablike creatures lurked within. The mud often stank. "No one likes the mangroves," John Steinbeck once wrote. And in Florida, until very recently, he was right. Few people complained as stands of mangroves along the state's southeast coast were replaced with sea-walled housing developments, hotels, and shopping plazas. pages.text: The world's glaciers are melting faster than we thought, new research shows | National Geographic Premium ENVIRONMENT The world's glaciers are melting faster than we thought, new research shows Glaciers have survived through a delicate balance of gain and loss. A new study shows just how much the scale has tipped. Drone light dramatically illuminates the Pastoruri Glacier in Cordillera Blanca, Peru. Glaciers like these provide drinking water to communities during their dry seasons. As they melt, this water supply dwindles and lost ice causes seas to rise. Photograph by Reuben Wu, Nat Geo Image Collection By Theo Nicitopoulos Published November 15, 2024 In 1971, researchers made a surprising discovery while studying Greenland's ice: Temperatures over the island spiked by very large amounts within short periods thousands of years ago. The finding showed that abrupt warming could happen over just several decades and changed how they thought about natural climate change. ( Arctic Ice Isn't Doomed Yet—Here's How to Save It) Today, the world is the in the grips of another major shift, this time due to anthropogenic activities. pages.text: This Four-Person NASA Crew Spent Over a Year on 'Mars.' Here's What They Did for 378 Days in a Simulated Martian Habitat Skip to main content Four individuals participated in NASA's second Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog (CHAPEA) mission. NASA / James Blair On October 31, four NASA crewmembers returned from “Mars.” Not the actual Red Planet, of course, but a 3D-printed Mars habitat in Houston where the three men and one woman lived for 378 days. Now, the Mars analog astronauts— Ross Elder , Ellen Ellis , James Spicer and Matthew Montgomery —have started telling the world what took place after they disappeared into NASA’s Mars Dune Alpha habitat at the Johnson Space Center on October 19, 2025, for the agency’s second Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog (CHAPEA) mission. The mission aimed to test the kinds of physical and mental conditions that a team of Mars explorers would endure on the Red Planet, including long-term isolation, disrupted communication with people on Earth and food cultivation. The habitat includes both a base and a mock outdoor environment , so the crew could practice Marswalks. “For more than a year, they have lived in an isolated environment, conducting critical research and helping us better understand what it will take to send humans to Mars,” Vanessa Wyche , director of NASA’s Johnson Space Center, said during a livestream , just before the crew emerged. “Inside just 1,700 square feet, they managed to live with limited resources. They maintained their habitat. They grew crops, and they carried out simulated Mars operations.”

Museum Wales In 1999, Peter Hughes stumbled upon the brass combination lock on Margam Beach in Wales. It featured four rotating dials, each bearing six letters. The dials turned smoothly, but only one of 1,296 possible combinations would open the device. The lock was an artifact from the Ann Francis , a merchant ship that sank in 1583. Hundreds of the vessel’s treasures—including compasses, coins and cannonballs—have since surfaced on the beach. But Hughes was particularly intrigued by the lock. He fiddled with the dials for two decades, trying to solve the puzzle. Now, researchers have used CT scans to reveal the four-letter code: ANCE. When they tested it out, the lock clicked open for the first time in more than four centuries. “For me, it’s like opening the Ark of the Covenant,” Hughes tells BBC Wales ’ Meleri Williams. “I’m delighted—truly thrilled.” The Ann Francis was traveling from Spain to England when a storm swept in on December 28, 1583. The winds blew it off course, and it ultimately wrecked off Margam Beach in southern Wales. According to a parish register, 14 sailors died in December 1583, and these men may have been the Ann Francis ’ crew. pages.description: Could Spinosaurus swim? A new fossil with a scimitar-like head crest provides new evidence on the unsettled question.
pages.text: This Odd-Looking New Spinosaurus Is Reviving an Age-Old Debate | National Geographic SCIENCE This Odd-Looking New Spinosaurus Is Reviving an Age-Old Debate Could Spinosaurus swim? A new fossil with a scimitar-like head crest provides new evidence on the unsettled question. Unearthed in a rare Saharan fossil site in Niger, Spinosaurus mirabilis had a large head crest that may have signaled a message to rivals competing for resources or territory along the way. artwork by Dani Navarro By Helen Thompson Published February 19, 2026 Under the central Saharan sun, paleontologist Daniel Vidal spotted a mysterious bone poking out of the ground during an excavation in Niger. It looked like a dinosaur vertebra at first. But upon further inspection, researchers realized the bone was a curved, sword-like crest that would have been attached to the skull of one of paleontology’s most oddball dinosaurs—the sail-backed predator Spinosaurus . “It was amazing,” recalls Vidal, of the University of Chicago. “It was like a unicorn.” Back in 2022, when he stumbled upon the strange bone, he was part of a team led by National Geographic Explorer Paul Sereno, a paleontologist also at Chicago , excavating a remote fossil site called Jenguebi. Now, the researchers report the crest belonged to an entirely new species— Spinosaurus mirabilis —that roamed the area’s ancient river ecosystem some 95 million years ago in the Late Cretaceous. They published their discovery Thursday in Science . The new species adds to a heated debate over how these puzzling (and popular) dinosaurs lived and hunted in water.

Photograph by Daniel Bourque, Alamy Stock Photo TRAVEL This stargazing road trip offers world-class night sky views Take a trip to Colorado, home to incredible stargazing sites—and what may become the world’s largest Dark Sky reserve. By Jacqueline Kehoe Published September 30, 2020 • 9 min read At few points in humanity’s past has seeing the Milky Way been a rare experience—until now. Eighty percent of Americans live under a hazy umbrella of light pollution. Even if we put away the screens long enough to look up, the glare of our existence blocks out the stars . The good news? There’s a growing idea that wilderness extends to the skies. Parks, communities, and sanctuaries certified by the International Dark-Sky Association are slowly popping up all across the country. If approved, Colorado’s proposed 3,000-square-mile Sangre de Cristo International Dark Sky Reserve would be the world’s largest dark-sky designated area. Even without the designation, the skies of Southwest Colorado—shielded from the interstate glow by endless mountains—blaze with stars. So hop in the car. This road trip takes you through the heart of the proposed reserve: far from crowds, through tiny mountain towns and deep into public lands. pages.text: This UK seaside town is a fossil hunter's paradise | National Geographic TRAVEL Why the U.K.'s fossil capital is the perfect seaside getaway Famed for its excellent fossil-hunting beaches, this Georgian town on Dorset’s Jurassic Coast offers plenty of seaside distractions, from paleontology walks to seafood feasts with a view. The harbour wall of Lyme Regis is also known as The Cobb. Thomas Faull, Getty Images By Jessica Prupas Published August 1, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). Were you to dig below Lyme Regis’ bunting-slung streets, you’d hit a geological marvel: the Blue Lias. This vast sequence of limestone and shale layers, formed during the Mesozoic era some 200 million years ago, reveals fossils as it erodes, making the town one of Europe’s most important paleontological centres. It’s a badge locals wear proudly: you’ll find a weather-beaten statue of celebrated fossil hunter Mary Anning overlooking Church Cliff Beach. In 1823, while wandering Lyme Regis’s coastline, she unearthed the world’s first complete skeleton of a Plesiosaurus and, nearly two centuries after her death, the town remains a magnet for excavators. Lyme Regis' seafront is a walkable promenade best discovered at dusk. Graham Custance, Getty Images Where should I begin? The main strip is Front Beach, which fringes the promenade with its wash of pastel huts. On its western end, you’ll find Shoreline Sauna , whose wood-fired, Nordic-style saunas sit right on the sand.
